references.descriptionFr: National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) - Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: What You Need to Know (current page). Central symptoms, impact, differential diagnosis and treatments of ADHD.
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) - ADHD in Adults (2026). Adult manifestations, functional impact, evaluation and follow-up.

National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) - Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management (NG87) (2018, current update). Assessment, shared plan, environmental adaptations and treatments for ADHD.
World Health Organization (WHO) - Doing what matters in times of stress: an illustrated guide (2020). Anchoring, defusion, welcoming of emotions, values ​​and brief actions.

Shaw, P., Stringaris, A., Nigg, J. and Leibenluft, E. - Emotion dysregulation in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (2014). Review on the frequency, impact and mechanisms of emotional dysregulation in ADHD.
Soler-Gutiérrez, A. M. et al. - Evidence of emotion dysregulation as a core symptom of adult ADHD: A systematic review (2023). Systematic review on emotional dysregulation in adults with ADHD.
Nordby, E. S. et al. - A Blended Intervention Targeting Emotion Dysregulation in Adults With ADHD (2024). Feasibility study; strategies reported useful and limitations of effectiveness data.

Liu, C. I. et al. - Effectiveness of cognitive behavioral-based interventions for adults with ADHD: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (2023). Effects of cognitive-behavioral interventions on central and emotional symptoms.
Young, Z., Moghaddam, N. and Tickle, A. - The Efficacy of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Adults With ADHD (2020). Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized trials of CBT in adults.

Lenzi, F. et al. - Pharmacotherapy of emotional dysregulation in adults with ADHD (2018). Systematic review and meta-analysis; the emotional effects of treatments cannot be deduced from the effects on central symptoms.
Hupfeld, K. E., Abagis, T. R. and Shah, P. - Living “in the zone”: hyperfocus in adult ADHD (2019). Descriptive study of hyperfocus; associated notion but not independent diagnostic criterion.
Malkovsky, E. et al. - Exploring the relationship between boredom and sustained attention (2012). Association between boredom propensity, sustained attention and adult ADHD symptoms.
Mette, C. - Time Perception in Adult ADHD: Findings from a Decade - A Review (2023). State of research on temporal perception and organization in adults.

Canu, W. H. and Carlson, C. L. - Rejection sensitivity and social outcomes of young adult men with ADHD (2007). Study on sensitivity to rejection and social results; limited data and no diagnosis of “RSD”.

Niermann, H. C. M. and Scheres, A. - The relationship between procrastination and symptoms of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in undergraduate students (2014). Association between symptoms of inattention and procrastination; correlational study.

Halmøy, A. et al. - Dialectical behavioral therapy-based group treatment versus treatment as usual for adults with ADHD (2022). Randomized trial of structured training inspired by DBT in adults with ADHD.

Fleming, A. P. et al. - Pilot randomized controlled trial of dialectical behavior therapy group skills training for ADHD among college students (2015). Pilot test of training in regulation and organization skills.
National Health Service (NHS) - Breathing exercises for stress (current page). Slow, unforced breathing as a simple tool to reduce activation.
Service-Public.fr - Emergency: who to call? (current page). Access to emergency services in France; elsewhere, use local services.
American Psychiatric Association - What is ADHD? (current page). Diagnostic benchmarks, impact and distinction with voluntarily oppositional behavior.

WORKING DEFINITION A difficulty can combine intense emotion, impulsivity, executive blockage, overload and time pressure. In the beginning, the exact label matters less than safety and the return of a minimum of choice.
Status	Universal transdiagnostic module. It does not prove ADHD or the ADHD origin of an episode.
Objective	Stabilize, postpone costly actions and then identify the dominant mechanism.
When to use it	When this experience dominates the wave or appears as its main driving force.
Typical cycle
1. A demand, obstacle or fatigue reduces capacity.
2. Attention narrows to the most salient emergency.
3. Several mechanisms overlap and become difficult to distinguish.
4. Immediate action promises rapid relief.
5. The cost of this action then maintains the wave.
Frequent triggers
Request accumulation	Unexpected change
Failure or obstacle	Criticism or ambiguous message
Time perceived as insufficient	Fatigue, hunger or overload
Possible events
Body	Voltage ; Restlessness or immobility; Short breathing; Need to move or flee
Thoughts	“Everything is urgent”; “I must act now”; Rapid, competing thoughts; Difficulty naming the problem
Emotions	Irritation; Panic ; Shame ; Discouragement
Behaviors	Switch from one action to another; Send or decide too quickly; Avoid ; Seek immediate stimulation
To be distinguished from: medical emergency; autistic overload; anxiety attack, mood episode or substance effect.

SAFETY SIGNAL intention or plan to harm oneself or do harm; fear of losing control, dangerous driving, threats or violence; confusion, very unusual agitation, worrying physical symptom or sudden change after treatment or substance. In these cases, prioritize human or medical help.

WORKING DEFINITION An obstacle, an expectation or an error can produce a very rapid emotional rise. ADHD can contribute through impulsivity and emotional regulation, but fatigue, pain, anxiety and context also matter.
Status	Practical profile associated with low frustration tolerance. It is not an official subtype of ADHD.
Objective	Create a pause between the obstacle and the reaction, then choose a proportionate response.
When to use it	When this experience dominates the wave or appears as its main driving force.
Typical cycle
1. An objective is blocked or delayed.
2. The delay is interpreted as an intolerable loss.
3. Body activation speeds up thoughts.
4. Forcing or attacking gives a feeling of regaining control.
5. Errors and damages add new frustration.
Frequent triggers
Queue or slowness	Repeated error
Malfunctioning tool	Interruption without solution
Fuzzy instruction	Results slower than expected
Possible events
Body	Jaw clenched; Heat ; Sudden gestures; Motor agitation
Thoughts	“It’s unbearable”; “It should already work”; “I’m wasting my time”; More and more radical solutions
Emotions	Irritation; Helplessness; Emergency ; Discouragement
Behaviors	Force; Repeat faster; Give up abruptly; Speaking sharply
Distinct from: acute pain or medical problem; sensory overload; relational anger or unusual episode of agitation.

UNDERSTAND	impulsive anger
This page is used to recognize the mechanism without diagnosing yourself. Read here outside of the crisis; during a climb, go directly to page 3 of the module.

WORKING DEFINITION Anger can build quickly, last longer than expected and cause people to speak or act before having dealt with the consequences. The objective is to secure, leave the duel and return only when behavioral control is reliable.
Status	Emotional dysregulation profile. Anger is not a stand-alone diagnostic criterion and ADHD never excuses threat, violence or control.
Objective	Prevent emotion from becoming a dangerous or relationally destructive action.
When to use it	When this experience dominates the wave or appears as its main driving force.
Typical cycle
1. An event is perceived as attack, injustice or obstruction.
2. The body quickly goes into confrontation mode.
3. Nuances and consequences become less accessible.
4. The strong expression provides an immediate discharge.
5. Fear, shame or secondary conflict then reignites anger.
Frequent triggers
Feeling of injustice	Limit or refusal
Review	Repeated interruption
Accumulation not expressed	Fatigue or drug rebound possible
Possible events
Body	Intense heat; Clenched fists or jaw; Tunnel vision; loud voice
Thoughts	“He must understand now”; “I am disrespected”; Punitive responses; Total certainty of being right
Emotions	Anger; Injury ; Humiliation; Impotence
Behaviors	Cut the floor; Send a burst of messages; Threaten to leave; Hitting an object or driving fast
To be distinguished from: real danger requiring protection; panic attack or overload; mania, intoxication, withdrawal or medical disorder.

SAFETY SIGNAL intention or plan to harm oneself or do harm; fear of losing control, dangerous driving, threats or violence; confusion, very unusual agitation, worrying physical symptom or sudden change after treatment or substance. In these cases, prioritize human or medical help.

contentLines: UNDERSTAND	criticism and rejection
This page is used to recognize the mechanism without diagnosing yourself. Read here outside of the crisis; during a climb, go directly to page 3 of the module.
WORKING DEFINITION A remark, silence or refusal can be experienced as a global condemnation. The reaction can range from shame, withdrawal, anger, or an urgent search for reassurance.
Status	Descriptive profile of rejection sensitivity. “Rejection-sensitive dysphoria” is not an official diagnosis or specific to ADHD.
Objective	Separate fact from interpretation and protect the link without requiring immediate certainty.
When to use it	When this experience dominates the wave or appears as its main driving force.
Typical cycle
1. A real or ambiguous social signal is detected.
2. The brain transforms it into a global and lasting judgment.
3. Shame, fear and activation reduce access to nuances.
4. Reassurance, flight or defense bring brief relief.
5. Repetition tires the connection and seems to confirm the initial fear.
Frequent triggers
Correction or negative feedback	Unanswered message
Refusal of a request	Social comparison
Change in tone	Error exposed in front of others
Possible events
Body	Energy drop; Chest pain or knotted stomach; Blushing; Want to disappear or flee
Thoughts	“They don’t want me anymore”; " I'm terrible " ; Mind reading; Search for ancient evidence
Emotions	Shame; Sadness; Fear ; Defensive anger
Behaviors	Apologize in succession; Request several guarantees; Withdraw abruptly; Counterattack
To be distinguished from: anxious attachment; social anxiety, depression or trauma; conflict or rejection actually established.

SAFETY SIGNAL intention or plan to harm oneself or do harm; fear of losing control, dangerous driving, threats or violence; confusion, very unusual agitation, worrying physical symptom or sudden change after treatment or substance. In these cases, prioritize human or medical help.

WORKING DEFINITION When too many elements remain active in the head, each new choice can cause the hierarchy to be lost. Stillness or restlessness does not mean that nothing is important; this may mean that everything is simultaneous.
Status	Executive overload profile. It can be linked to ADHD but also to exhaustion, ASD, anxiety or an objectively excessive situation.

Inbox full	Choice with too many options
Conflicting instructions	Cluttered space or desk

WORKING DEFINITION Time can remain abstract and then suddenly become a concrete emergency. The delay, deadline or accumulation then triggers acceleration, unrealistic promises and additional errors.
Status	Practical profile associated with time management and perception. These difficulties are neither universal nor specific to ADHD.

When to use it	When this experience dominates the wave or appears as its main driving force.

1. Future time remains imprecise or poorly estimated.

3. Panic leads to keeping too many goals.
4. Rushing and transitions increase errors.

Imminent departure	Deadline discovered late
Duration underestimation	Forgotten prerequisites
Successive delays	Multiple deadlines on the same day

Thoughts	“I can still do everything”; “It’s ruined”; Changing calculations; Promises of extreme catch-up
Emotions	Panic; Shame ; Irritation; Despair
Behaviors	Run or drive fast; Skipping meals or treatment; Hide the delay; Start several catch-ups

WORKING DEFINITION Anger, frustration or shame find no acceptable target and turn against the body, needs, projects or reputation. Punishment sometimes gives a feeling of control.
Status	Set of behaviors and impulses, not autonomous diagnosis. Any self-harm or suicidal intent requires a safety assessment.
Objective	Interrupt the damage, identify the anger and convert it into a limit, repair or safe discharge.
When to use it	When this experience dominates the wave or appears as its main driving force.
